name: Brand Under Pressure — Zuriel Foods' 5-Day Reputation Crisis
description: A four-round, advanced corporate-brand and crisis-communication simulation set inside Zuriel Foods Plc., a listed Nigerian FMCG (NGN 84bn revenue, 2,300 staff, #2 seasoning brand at 24% share) built since 1991 on one promise: "Nourishing Nigerian families." On Thursday 14 May 2026 a consumer influencer alleges the flagship seasoning hides an undeclared additive; the video hits 2.4M views in 18 hours, #ZurielExposed trends, two retail chains (31% of modern-trade volume) delist, week-one sales fall 22%, 89% of mentions turn negative, and the corporate-reputation tracker drops from 72 to 51 in 72 hours. The firm's own lab needs 5 days; the response must be locked first. Playing the Brand Director with a NGN 600M contingency budget, you treat the corporate brand as socially constructed (Otubanjo) and manage the coherence between projected identity, actual substance, and stakeholders' construed image. Round 1 — diagnose the crisis as a coherence failure, locating the gap between the stated 'all-natural' identity, the permitted-but-undisclosed additive (the say-do gap), and the construed image, and separating a genuine substance problem from a perception problem. Round 2 — align the identity before communicating: defend 'all-natural' and reformulate, reframe to 'safe, transparent, trusted' with full disclosure, hold and contest on facts, or reposition around heritage — and decide whether substance must change to make the new identity true. Round 3 — allocate the NGN 600M across a menu (CEO statement, independent third-party lab certification, influencer & retailer re-engagement, paid corrective advertising, a transparency microsite with batch traceability, frontline briefing), sequence it against the 5-day window, choose spokesperson and tone, and keep messages consistent across consumers, retailers, the NAFDAC regulator, employees and investors — because inconsistency itself signals evasion. Round 4 — the facilitator reveals the lab result (clean or a minor confirmed deviation) and you must hold a coherent repositioning that rebuilds reputation over a quarter without erasing 35 years of equity, then pitch the board and a skeptical journalist. The math rewards substance-before-message, credibility (certification, traceability) over reach, stakeholder coherence, calibrated response under uncertainty, and trust repair even when vindicated — and punishes the five classic errors: messaging over an open say-do gap, premature defiance, divergent stakeholder messages, buying reach instead of proof, and panic repositioning. Final KPIs: Reputation tracker (0–100), Perceived Consistency (0–100), Sales Recovery (% vs pre-crisis), and Negative Share-of-Voice (%, lower better).

Brand Under Pressure

You are the Brand Director of a 35-year-old Nigerian food company whose entire premium positioning rests on the promise “Nourishing Nigerian families.” A viral safety allegation has punctured a reputation built since 1991. With a ₦600M budget and five days, realign what the brand actually stands for, choose where to spend on credibility, and rebuild trust — before the lab result returns and before public belief hardens.

Round 1 — Diagnose the reputation gap

Your Decisions This Round

Genuine substance problem: 50%
The additive is real but permitted and undisclosed — part substance (the say–do gap), part perception (the viral belief). Naming it as 100% perception denies the real gap; 100% substance over-states a permitted ingredient.
Consistency with “Nourishing Nigerian families since 1991”: 50
Reputation is built on consistency over time. A coherent evolution preserves equity; an overnight rebrand confuses the loyal consumers you are trying to save.
Independent third-party lab certification (slow, highest credibility, proof not slogan)
Transparency microsite with batch traceability (fast proof, lets people check for themselves)
CEO video statement (credible spokesperson, fast, sets the tone)
Influencer & retailer re-engagement (relist the shelf, turn the narrative)
Paid corrective advertising (maximum reach, low proof — “trust us” at volume)
Frontline & retail-staff briefing (employees and shelves tell one story)
Budget allocated: 600 / ₦600M
Stakeholder message consistency: 50
The lab result is about to return…
Effort on trust repair after the result: 50%
Being right is not the same as being trusted again — 60% of consumers who saw the video never saw the clean result, and two retailers still have not relisted.
Facilitator (the board chair & a skeptical journalist)
Three things are now out of alignment: what Zuriel says it is, what the product actually is, and what 2.4 million people believe. A corporate brand is what stakeholders believe it to be — you cannot message your way out of an identity that no longer holds. Before you spend a Naira, decide what Zuriel truly stands for; then buy proof, not volume; and keep one story for everyone. I am writing this whether you talk to me or not.
